technical.prompt: What is a financial restructuring?
expectedPoints: Changing a company's debt and capital structure to address financial distress
Can include reducing debt, extending maturities or converting debt into equity
Can happen out of court or through a court process
Often combined with operational changes

choices.answer: Changing a distressed company's capital structure to make it viable
distractors: Changing a company's board after an election
Moving a company to a new country for tax
Splitting a company's shares into more shares

technical.prompt: What is the difference between a Chapter 11 and a Chapter 7 bankruptcy?
expectedPoints: Chapter 11 is a reorganisation; the business keeps operating
Management usually stays in control and proposes a plan
Chapter 7 is a liquidation
In Chapter 7, a trustee sells the assets and distributes the proceeds

choices.answer: Chapter 11 reorganises the business; Chapter 7 liquidates it
distractors: Chapter 11 liquidates the business; Chapter 7 reorganises it
Chapter 11 is for individuals; Chapter 7 for companies
They differ only in which court hears the case

technical.prompt: What is the automatic stay?
expectedPoints: Takes effect immediately when a company files
Stops most creditor collection efforts, lawsuits and foreclosures
Gives the company breathing room to reorganise
Creditors can ask the court to lift it in some cases

choices.answer: An immediate halt on most creditor collection actions after filing
distractors: A freeze on the company's share price
A ban on the company paying employees
A delay of the court's first hearing

technical.prompt: What is debtor-in-possession financing?
expectedPoints: New financing provided to a company during Chapter 11
Requires court approval
Usually has super-priority status
Funds operations and restructuring costs

choices.answer: Court-approved new financing for a company in Chapter 11
distractors: Loans the company made before filing
Equity invested by the company's founders
A government grant for distressed firms

technical.prompt: What is the absolute priority rule?
expectedPoints: Senior claims must be paid in full before junior claims receive anything
Applies when a plan is imposed on a dissenting class
Equity holders are last in line
Deviations usually need consent of the affected classes

choices.answer: Senior claims are paid in full before junior claims get anything
distractors: All creditors are paid the same percentage
Equity holders are paid first to keep them invested
The largest creditor is always paid first

technical.prompt: What are the early warning signs that a company is heading into financial distress?
expectedPoints: Falling liquidity and cash burn
Covenant breaches or waivers
Declining EBITDA and rising leverage
Bonds trading at deep discounts
Suppliers tightening payment terms and auditor going-concern warnings

technical.prompt: Why does a covenant breach matter so much for a struggling company?
expectedPoints: It is an event of default
Lenders can demand repayment or impose new terms
Can trigger defaults on other debt
Gives lenders leverage in negotiations

choices.answer: It is a default that gives lenders the right to act
distractors: It automatically cancels the company's debt
It lowers the interest rate on the loan
It only affects the company's credit rating

technical.prompt: What are the pros and cons of an out-of-court restructuring compared with a court process?
expectedPoints: Out of court is usually cheaper, faster and more private
It causes less disruption to customers and suppliers

Holdouts cannot be forced to agree, which a court process can do

choices.answer: Cheaper and faster, but it cannot force holdouts to agree
distractors: More expensive, but it binds all creditors
Slower, but it requires no creditor consent
Identical cost, but only equity holders vote

technical.prompt: What is a distressed exchange?
expectedPoints: Creditors swap existing debt for new securities
The new package is usually worth less than the old debt's face value
May include lower principal, longer maturity or equity

choices.answer: Swapping debt for new securities worth less than face value
distractors: Trading shares on a distressed stock exchange
Selling assets to pay off lenders in full
Refinancing debt at a lower rate with full repayment

technical.prompt: What is a Section 363 sale?
expectedPoints: A sale of assets during Chapter 11 with court approval
Assets are sold free and clear of liens and claims
Can be completed quickly
Proceeds go to creditors according to priority

choices.answer: A court-approved asset sale free of liens during Chapter 11
distractors: A sale of shares to the public before bankruptcy
A tax-free spin-off of a division
A sale approved only by shareholders

technical.prompt: What is a plan of reorganisation?

The auditor's report on past accounts

technical.prompt: What is the fulcrum security?

choices.answer: The class where value runs out; it usually gets the new equity
distractors: The most senior secured loan, always repaid in full
The company's common stock, which is always wiped out
The security with the highest coupon in the structure

technical.prompt: What is a 13-week cash flow forecast?

technical.prompt: Who are the main stakeholders in a restructuring?

Shareholders

How long a court case will last

technical.prompt: What is a prepackaged bankruptcy?

distractors: A liquidation completed in a single day

technical.prompt: What does it mean for a DIP loan to prime existing liens, and what is adequate protection?

technical.prompt: What vote is needed for a class of creditors to accept a plan in Chapter 11?

technical.prompt: How do you value a company in a restructuring?

Comparable companies applied to normalised EBITDA
Liquidation analysis as a floor
Precedent transactions, where relevant
